idiom_name: sqlite3 INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING + rowcount
implementation_notes: The durable idiom needs no dependency: sqlite3 ships with CPython, so one deduplication table with a UNIQUE key plus `INSERT OR IGNORE` (or `ON CONFLICT(key) DO NOTHING`) and `cursor.rowcount == 1` is the atomic claim, with the business writes in the same transaction. Postgres/psycopg and Django's get_or_create follow the same shape on a unique index. Choose it whenever redelivery can outlive the process or several workers (gunicorn, Celery) consume the same queue.
code_sketch:
with conn:                                     # one transaction
    cur = conn.execute(
        "INSERT INTO seen(key, at) VALUES(?, ?) ON CONFLICT(key) DO NOTHING",
        (msg.key, time.time()))
    if cur.rowcount == 0:
        return ack(msg)                        # duplicate: absorb, do not reprocess
    apply_effects(conn, msg)
ack(msg)
pitfalls: cursor.rowcount is only meaningful for the claim statement itself; check it before reusing the connection for business writes.
Only a zero-row claim insert is a duplicate - a transient database error must propagate so the broker redelivers.
The dedup table grows; delete rows older than the redelivery window on a schedule.

variants.name: Distributed claim with redis-py SET NX PX
variants.implementation_notes: redis-py maps `set(name, value, nx=True, px=ttl)` onto the single `SET key value NX PX ttl` command: the first caller gets True, later callers get None, and the TTL arms expiry in the same round trip. That is the standard distributed claim for several Python processes; None means duplicate, while connection errors must be retried rather than absorbed.
pitfalls: Only the NX result distinguishes duplicate from failure; a raised ConnectionError must not be swallowed as a duplicate.
TTL shorter than the broker's redelivery window reopens duplicates after expiry.

variants.name: In-process set guard (single process)
variants.implementation_notes: `if key in seen: return False; seen.add(key)` is atomic only because CPython's GIL makes the two bytecodes effectively uninterruptible in one thread - it is still not safe with multiple worker processes, fork-based servers or restarts, and other threads can interleave unless a Lock wraps the pair. Appropriate only for a single-process receiver; use the durable claim otherwise. `dict.setdefault` is the one-call variant of the same shape.
pitfalls: The guard evaporates on restart and is invisible to sibling worker processes.
A blocking or async yield between check and add reintroduces the race the pair was standing in for.
